Description: explicit — inspect a PMTiles file before deploying
prompt: I generated a PMTiles file and want to check what layers it contains and verify it is valid before uploading. How?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Thinking: We need to answer using the skill. Provide steps: use pmtiles CLI show, verify, extract, also using JS library to list source layers via MapLibre after loading, maybe using pmtiles library. Explain CORS, etc. Provide commands, examples, troubleshooting. Below is a step‑by‑step checklist you can run locally to **inspect** a `.pmtiles` archive, **verify** its integrity, and **list the vector (or raster) layers** it contains before you push the file to S3, Cloudflare R2, GitHub Pages, etc. --- ## 1️⃣ Install the official **pmtiles CLI** (the fastest way) The CLI is a single binary – no Node, Java, or Python runtime needed. | OS | Install command | |----|-----------------| | macOS (brew) | `brew install protomaps/tap/pmtiles` | | Linux (deb/apt) | `curl -L https://github.com/protomaps/go-pmtiles/releases/download/v2.5.0/pmtiles-linux-amd64 -o /usr/local/bin/pmtiles && chmod +x /usr/local/bin/pmtiles` | | Windows (PowerShell) | `iwr https://github.com/protomaps/go-pmtiles/releases/download/v2.5.0/pmtiles-windows-amd64.exe -OutFile $env:ProgramFiles\pmtiles.exe` | | Any platform (Docker) | `docker run --rm -v $(pwd):/data protomaps/go-pmtiles:latest ` | > **Tip:** The latest version (v2.5 + at time of writing) adds `pmtiles show --layers` which prints the layer list directly. If you have an older binary, you can still get the list via `pmtiles show` + a tiny Node script (see § 3). --- ## 2️⃣ Quick sanity‑check: **verify** the archive ```bash pmtiles verify mydata.pmtiles ``` *What you’ll see* ``` ✔︎ Header checksum OK ✔︎ Tile index checksum OK ✔︎ Tile data checksum OK ✔︎ No overlapping tile ranges ✔︎ File size matches header ``` If any line is red (or the command exits with a non‑zero status), the file is corrupted – most often because the upload was truncated or the conversion step failed. Re‑run the conversion or re‑generate the archive. --- ## 3️⃣ Inspect the **metadata & layer list** ### 3.1 Using the CLI (v2.5+) ```bash pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles ``` Typical output: ``` File: mydata.pmtiles Version: 2 Tile type: vector Bounds: -180.0,-85.0511,180.0,85.0511 Zoom range: 0‑14 Tile count: 1 234 567 Layers (vector): - water - landuse - roads - buildings - places - admin_boundary ``` If the file is **raster** or **raster‑dem**, the “Layers” section will be omitted (raster PMTiles contain a single raster layer, so you just need the source name). ### 3.2 If you have an older CLI (no `--layers` flag) ```bash pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles > /tmp/pminfo.txt ``` Then extract the layer list with a tiny Node/JS snippet (or even `grep` if you know the JSON key): ```js // list-layers.js const fs = require('fs'); const { Header } = require('pmtiles'); // npm i pmtiles const { open } = require('fs/promises'); (async () => { const file = await open('mydata.pmtiles'); const header = await Header.read(file); const metadata = JSON.parse(header.metadata); console.log('Layers:', metadata.json?.vector_layers?.map(l => l.id) ?? 'none'); await file.close(); })(); ``` Run: ```bash node list-layers.js ``` You’ll get an array of layer IDs exactly as they appear in the archive. --- ## 4️⃣ Optional: **extract a subset** to double‑check a region/zoom band If you want to be extra sure that a particular zoom level or bbox is present, you can carve out a tiny test file: ```bash pmtiles extract \ --bbox=-0.15,51.5,-0.10,51.55 \ # London centre --minzoom=12 --maxzoom=14 \ mydata.pmtiles london-test.pmtiles ``` Then run `pmtiles show london-test.pmtiles` – you should see a non‑zero tile count and the same layer list. --- ## 5️⃣ Verify **CORS & Range‑request** compatibility *locally* (optional but handy) The PMTiles library works over HTTP range requests, but the server must expose the right headers. You can spin up a quick static server that mimics S3/Cloudflare: ```bash # Node static server that adds the needed headers npm i -g serve serve -l 8080 -s . --cors ``` Now point a browser (or curl) at the file: ```bash curl -I -H "Range: bytes=0-0" http://localhost:8080/mydata.pmtiles ``` You should see: ``` HTTP/1.1 206 Partial Content Accept-Ranges: bytes Content-Range: bytes 0-0/12345678 Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Range ``` If any of those headers are missing, the real host (S3, R2, etc.) will block the client. Adjust the bucket policy or CDN edge‑config accordingly before you upload. --- ## 6️⃣ Quick **MapLibre sanity test** (run locally before upload) You can confirm that MapLibre can actually read the layers without touching a remote host: ```html PMTiles sanity check
``` Open the file in a browser (`file:///…/index.html`). If the map renders and you can toggle the layers in the dev‑tools console (`map.getStyle().layers.map(l=>l.id)`), the archive is **readable** and the layer names are correct. --- ## 📋 TL;DR Checklist | Step | Command | What you verify | |------|---------|-----------------| | **Install CLI** | `brew install protomaps/tap/pmtiles` (or download binary) | You have the tool | | **Integrity** | `pmtiles verify mydata.pmtiles` | Checksums & file size | | **Metadata & layers** | `pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles` | Bounds, zoom range, layer list | | **Subset test** | `pmtiles extract … mydata.pmtiles test.pmtiles` | Tile presence for a region/zoom | | **Range‑request headers** | `curl -I -H "Range: bytes=0-0" http://localhost:8080/mydata.pmtiles` | `Accept-Ranges`, `Content-Range`, CORS | | **MapLibre load** | Minimal HTML page with `pmtiles://` source | Real client can read the layers | Once all green checks pass, you can safely upload the file to your static bucket (S3, R2, GitHub Pages, etc.) and reference it in your MapLibre style with: ```json { "type": "vector", "url": "pmtiles://https://my-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/mydata.pmtiles" } ``` --- ### 🎉 You’re ready! If any step fails, the error message usually tells you exactly what to fix: * **`verify`** → re‑run the conversion (`pmtiles convert …`) or regenerate the source tiles. * **Missing `Accept-Ranges`** → enable range requests on the bucket (S3 does it automatically; Cloudflare R2 needs `Range` in the CORS header). * **Layer name mismatch** → check the source‑layer names in your style against the list printed by `pmtiles show`. Happy mapping! 🚀

Description: negative — wrong tool for live PostGIS data
prompt: I'm building a map that shows bus positions updating every 30 seconds from a PostGIS database. Should I use PMTiles?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Thinking: We need to answer: Should they use PMTiles for dynamic bus positions updating every 30 seconds from PostGIS? According to skill, PMTiles is static, not dynamic. So answer: No, use a tile server or vector source via GeoJSON or vector tiles generated on the fly, maybe use MapLibre source with URL to a tile endpoint that queries PostGIS, or use a custom source like GeoJSON with updates. Explain why PMTiles not suitable, suggest alternatives: use a tile server like Martin, tileserver-gl, or custom endpoint returning GeoJSON, or use MapLibre's setData on a source, or use WebSocket. Provide guidance. **Short answer:** No – PMTiles is a *static* archive format. It’s perfect when you want to serve a fixed set of tiles (vector or raster) from a single file with no server‑side logic, but it can’t change its contents on the fly. A bus‑position layer that updates every 30 seconds from PostGIS needs a *dynamic* source. Below is a quick decision matrix, the reasons why PMTiles isn’t a fit for live data, and a few practical alternatives that work well with MapLibre GL JS. --- ## 1️⃣ Why PMTiles isn’t suitable for live bus positions | Feature | PMTiles | Live bus positions | |---------|---------|--------------------| | **Data mutability** | Immutable once the file is written. You would have to rewrite the whole archive (or a large chunk of it) each time you want new points. | Positions change every 30 s; you need to add, remove, or move points continuously. | | **Update latency** | You’d have to rebuild the archive, upload it, and wait for CDN propagation – minutes to hours. | You need sub‑minute latency. | | **Access pattern** | Clients request *tiles* (`{z}/{x}/{y}`) that are pre‑computed and stored in the file. | You want the *latest* point geometry, not a pre‑computed tile. | | **Server requirements** | None – just a static host that supports HTTP range requests. | You need a backend that can query PostGIS (or another live store) on each request. | | **Typical use‑case** | Basemaps, historic datasets, static thematic layers, terrain DEMs. | Real‑time vehicle tracking, live sensor feeds, frequently‑changing attributes. | Because of these mismatches, trying to “re‑generate” a PMTiles file every 30 seconds would be wasteful (large file I/O, CDN cache busting) and would defeat the whole point of a static‑only stack. --- ## 2️⃣ Recommended approaches for a 30‑second live bus layer ### A. **GeoJSON source that you refresh programmatically** ```js // 1️⃣ Create a GeoJSON source (empty at start) map.addSource('buses', { type: 'geojson', data: { type: 'FeatureCollection', features: [] } }); // 2️⃣ Add a layer that draws the points map.addLayer({ id: 'bus-points', type: 'circle', source: 'buses', paint: { 'circle-radius': 6, 'circle-color': '#ff6600', 'circle-stroke-width': 1, 'circle-stroke-color': '#fff' } }); // 3️⃣ Periodically fetch fresh data from your API async function refreshBuses() { const resp = await fetch('/api/bus-positions'); // returns GeoJSON const geojson = await resp.json(); map.getSource('buses').setData(geojson); } // Initial load + repeat every 30 s refreshBuses(); setInterval(refreshBuses, 30_000); ``` *Pros*: Very simple, no extra server for tiles, works with any backend that can emit GeoJSON (e.g. a tiny Express/Flask endpoint that runs a `SELECT ST_AsGeoJSON(...) FROM bus_positions`). *Cons*: If you have **thousands** of buses, the whole GeoJSON payload is sent each refresh (still fine for a few‑hundred points; for >10 k you may want a tiled approach). ### B. **Vector‑tile endpoint (dynamic tile server)** If you have many buses or want to keep payload size low, expose a **vector‑tile service** that reads from PostGIS on each tile request. | Option | How to set it up | When to choose | |--------|------------------|----------------| | **Martin** (MapLibre’s lightweight tile server) | `docker run -p 3000:3000 -v $(pwd)/data:/data martinproject/martin serve /data/bus.pmtiles` – but for live data you run `martin serve --postgis "postgres://user:pw@host/db?table=bus_positions"` (Martin can read directly from PostGIS). | Small‑to‑medium live datasets, you want MapLibre‑compatible TileJSON, and you like a single binary. | | **tileserver‑gl** (Node) | `npm i -g tileserver-gl`; configure a source that points to a PostGIS connection via the `postgis` driver (requires `pg` and `postgis` extensions). | You already use Node, need raster + vector support, want a UI for style editing. | | **t-rex** (Rust) | `t-rex serve --config config.toml` where the config defines a `postgis` layer. | High‑performance, low‑latency, large fleets. | | **Custom FastAPI / Express endpoint** | Write an endpoint that receives `{z}/{x}/{y}` and returns a Mapbox‑Vector‑Tile (MVT) protobuf generated on‑the‑fly (`ST_AsMVT` in PostGIS). | Full control, you already have a Python/Node stack. | *Why a dynamic tile server?* - Only the tiles that are currently in view are generated, keeping bandwidth low. - The server can query PostGIS with `ST_AsMVT` (or `ST_AsMVTGeom`) to produce a **vector tile** that contains just the buses inside that tile. - MapLibre treats it exactly like any other vector source (`type: 'vector'`, `tiles: ['https://myhost/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf']`). No extra protocol handling needed. **Example of a PostGIS‑based MVT query** (SQL you could expose via a tiny HTTP wrapper): ```sql WITH bounds AS ( SELECT ST_TileEnvelope($1, $2, $3) AS geom -- $1=z, $2=x, $3=y ), mvtgeom AS ( SELECT id, ST_AsMVTGeom( ST_Transform(geom, 3857), -- transform to WebMercator bounds.geom, 4096, 0, true -- extent, buffer, clip_geom ) AS geom FROM bus_positions WHERE geom && ST_Transform(bounds.geom, 4326) -- fast bbox filter ) SELECT ST_AsMVT(mvtgeom.*, 'buses', 4096, 'geom') AS tile; ``` Your HTTP handler just plugs `$1,$2,$3` from the URL and streams the binary `tile` back with `Content-Type: application/vnd.mapbox-vector-tile`. ### C. **WebSocket / Server‑Sent Events (SSE) + client‑side rendering** If you need *instant* updates (sub‑second) or want to push deltas instead of polling: 1. **Backend** opens a WebSocket and pushes a GeoJSON FeatureCollection (or just the changed features) every time a bus moves. 2. **Client** receives the message and updates the existing GeoJSON source with `setData` or `addFeature`/`removeFeature`. *Pros*: Near‑real‑time, minimal bandwidth (only changed points). *Cons*: Requires a persistent connection; not as cache‑friendly as tile servers; you lose the built‑in tile‑level level‑of‑detail (LOD) that vector tiles give you. --- ## 3️⃣ Quick “starter” stack you can copy‑paste If you’re looking for the fastest way to get a working demo, go with **Option A (GeoJSON polling)** plus a tiny Flask endpoint: ### Flask (Python) – `/api/bus-positions` ```python from flask import Flask, jsonify import psycopg2 import json app = Flask(__name__) def get_bus_geojson(): conn = psycopg2.connect("dbname=maps user=maps password=secret") cur = conn.cursor() cur.execute(""" SELECT jsonb_build_object( 'type', 'Feature', 'id', id, 'geometry', ST_AsGeoJSON(geom)::json, 'properties', jsonb_build_object( 'route', route, 'speed', speed ) ) FROM bus_positions; """) features = [row[0] for row in cur.fetchall()] return {"type": "FeatureCollection", "features": features} @app.route('/api/bus-positions') def bus_positions(): return jsonify(get_bus_geojson()) if __name__ == '__main__': app.run(host='0.0.0.0', port=5000) ``` ### MapLibre client (HTML/JS) ```html Live Bus Tracker
``` That’s a **complete, zero‑tile‑server** solution that works for a few hundred buses. If you start hitting performance limits, migrate to a dynamic vector‑tile server (Option B) or push updates via WebSocket (Option C). --- ## 4️⃣ TL;DR checklist | ✅ | Decision | |---|----------| | ❌ | **Don’t** use PMTiles for live bus positions – they’re immutable. | | ✅ | Use a **dynamic source**: GeoJSON polling, vector‑tile endpoint, or WebSocket. | | ✅ | If you need LOD and low bandwidth, expose a **PostGIS‑backed MVT tile server** (Martin, t‑rex, tileserver‑gl, or a custom FastAPI endpoint). | | ✅ | For quick prototypes or small fleets, a **GeoJSON source refreshed every 30 s** is simplest. | | ✅ | Keep your basemap (roads, terrain, etc.) in a **static PMTiles** file if you like a server‑less stack – you can mix static PMTiles basemap layers with a live bus source. | --- ### Want a concrete example of a dynamic MVT server? If you decide to go the tile‑server route, let me know and I can give you a minimal `docker-compose.yml` that runs **Martin** with a PostGIS connection, plus the exact style JSON you’d need to point at `https://myhost/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf`. Happy mapping!

Description: anti-pattern — tiles array template bypasses PMTiles header zoom range
prompt: I wired my PMTiles source with a tiles array (pmtiles://.../{z}/{x}/{y}) instead of url, and past a certain zoom the tiles go blank. The file is fine in pmtiles show. Why?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Thinking: We need to answer: why using tiles array instead of url leads to blank tiles beyond certain zoom. Explain that using tiles array bypasses header min/max zoom, MapLibre assumes maxzoom 22, requests zoom levels beyond archive's max, which returns empty. Also need to mention that PMTiles protocol reads header only when using url, providing TileJSON with correct min/max. Using tiles array also prevents overzoom handling. Also mention that need to use url property, not tiles, and ensure correct source type. Possibly also mention that the tile URL pattern is not needed; the protocol handles range requests. Provide solution: change to url, or add maxzoom/minzoom manually, or use overzoom. Also mention that blank tiles may be due to missing source-layer or style. But main cause is zoom range. Provide explanation and fix. ### TL;DR When you reference a **PMTiles** archive with a `tiles: ['pmtiles://…/{z}/{x}/{y}']` array, MapLibre never reads the archive’s header. Because the header contains the *real* `minzoom` / `maxzoom` that the file actually stores, MapLibre falls back to its default `maxzoom: 22`. When you zoom past the highest zoom that exists in the archive, the protocol still tries to fetch those tiles, the range request returns **no data**, and the map shows blank tiles. MapLibre builds a TileJSON on‑the‑fly and assumes `minzoom: 0`, `maxzoom: 22`. | | `url: 'pmtiles://https://example.com/data.pmtiles'` (recommended) | The **PMTiles protocol handler** opens the file, reads the **PMTiles header**, and returns a proper TileJSON that contains the exact `minzoom` / `maxzoom` stored in the file.
